questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate. How does increasing the substrate concentration affect the rate of reaction in the presence of a competitive inhibitor?

options.text: It has no effect -- the inhibitor always blocks the enzyme
The rate decreases further because more substrate increases inhibitor binding
The rate increases because substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for the active site
The enzyme is denatured by the extra substrate

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the active site. By increasing substrate concentration, there are more substrate molecules relative to inhibitor molecules, so the substrate is more likely to bind to the active site. This means the inhibition can be overcome by high substrate concentration.

questions.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor binds to a site on the enzyme away from the active site. Why does this still reduce enzyme activity?

options.text: It destroys the enzyme permanently
It changes the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer fit
It blocks the substrate from reaching the enzyme
It increases the activation energy of the reaction

questions.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors bind to an allosteric site (not the active site), but this binding causes a conformational change in the enzyme that alters the shape of the active site. The substrate can no longer bind effectively, reducing the rate of reaction. Unlike competitive inhibition, this cannot be overcome by adding more substrate.

questions.stem: Many nerve agents (such as sarin) are irreversible enzyme inhibitors that permanently block acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. What effect would this have on the nervous system?

options.text: Nerve signals would stop completely
Acetylcholine would accumulate at synapses, causing continuous nerve stimulation and muscle contraction
The body would produce more acetylcholinesterase to compensate
Nerve impulses would travel faster

questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down acetylcholine after it has transmitted a nerve impulse across a synapse. If this enzyme is irreversibly inhibited, acetylcholine accumulates and continuously stimulates the post-synaptic neurone, leading to uncontrolled muscle contraction, paralysis, and potentially death.

questions.stem: End-product inhibition is a type of non-competitive inhibition where the product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an enzyme earlier in the pathway. Why is this biologically useful?

options.text: It prevents the cell from running out of substrate
It prevents wasteful overproduction of the end product, regulating the metabolic pathway
It speeds up the reaction when product levels are high
It permanently stops the pathway

questions.explanation: End-product inhibition is a form of negative feedback. When enough product has been made, it inhibits an early enzyme in the pathway, slowing or stopping production. When product levels fall (as the product is used up), the inhibition is released and the pathway resumes. This prevents wasting resources on unnecessary production.

questions.stem: Statins are drugs used to treat high cholesterol. They act as competitive inhibitors of the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, which is involved in cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Why must patients take statins regularly?

options.text: Statins permanently destroy the enzyme
Competitive inhibition is reversible, so the statin is eventually displaced and must be replaced
Statins are broken down into cholesterol over time
The liver stops producing the enzyme after taking statins

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly to the active site. Over time, the statin molecules are metabolised and excreted, allowing the enzyme to function again and resume cholesterol production. Regular doses maintain a sufficient concentration of the inhibitor to keep cholesterol synthesis suppressed.
